Akota: An important centre for Jain bronze sculpture

Akota, near Vadodara, formerly known as Baroda, is important in the history of Jain art because of a well-known collection of early medieval Jain bronze images found there.

The Akota bronzes demonstrate that Gujarat had an established tradition of producing metal religious images during the early medieval period. The group includes representations of Jain Tirthankaras and related religious figures.

The NCERT discussion of Jain temple architecture places important Akota bronzes between approximately the late 5th and late 7th centuries CE, while its discussion of Indian bronze sculpture describes the broader bronze-casting tradition at Akota over approximately the 6th–9th centuries CE. The useful core fact is their association with early medieval Jain metal sculpture in the Vadodara region.

What the bronzes represent

Among the Tirthankaras represented in the Akota bronze tradition are Adinatha, Parshvanatha and Mahavira. Jain bronze images could show a single Tirthankara or multiple Tirthankaras arranged together.

Many of these metal images were made using the lost-wax casting process. In this method, a wax model is used to form a mould, after which the wax is removed and molten metal takes its place. Some Akota bronzes also show details enhanced with other metals, including silver and copper.

The importance of these bronzes is artistic and religious. They are evidence of skilled metalworking connected with Jain image-making, and they form part of Gujarat's contribution to Indian sculptural traditions.

Akota and Valabhi represent different kinds of heritage

Akota near Vadodara: Jain bronze sculpture.
Valabhi: compilation and preservation of Shvetambara canonical texts.
Both are important to Gujarat's Jain history, but they are not the same centre or type of cultural activity.

Jainism's contribution to Gujarat's culture

Religious life and ethical ideas

The Jain emphasis on ahimsa contributed to the wider Indian discussion of non-violence and ethical conduct. In Gujarat, Jain communities maintained practices of worship, pilgrimage and religious discipline over many centuries.

Architecture and sculpture

The temple complexes of Shatrunjaya, Girnar, Taranga, Shankheshwar and Kumbhariya illustrate the geographical spread of Jain religious institutions across Gujarat. Monumental temple building and the production of smaller bronze images represent different branches of Jain artistic patronage.

Literature and learning

The textual tradition associated with Valabhi, the scholarship of Hemachandra and the later manuscript collections of Patan, Khambhat and Ahmedabad demonstrate Jainism's contribution to the preservation and development of religious and literary knowledge.

Trade, patronage and craftsmanship

Jain merchants, ministers and other wealthy donors supported religious construction and learning. Their patronage gave work to artists, builders, sculptors, scribes and painters. The connection between commercial prosperity and religious giving is therefore an important part of Gujarat's medieval social and cultural history.

Putting the entire subtopic together

For understanding and revision, Gujarat's Jain heritage can be organised into a few clear relationships. The pilgrimage centres are identified by their locations and associated Tirthankaras. The literary centres are identified by councils, scholars and manuscript repositories. The artistic heritage includes stone temples, marble carving, bronze images and manuscript painting. The patronage tradition connects rulers, ministers, merchants and other donors with these achievements.

The distinction between these categories is essential. Palitana should suggest Shatrunjaya and Adinatha; Girnar should suggest Neminatha; Taranga should suggest Ajitanatha; Valabhi should suggest the Shvetambara canonical compilation; Patan should suggest Hemachandra and Jain learning; and Akota should suggest Jain bronze sculpture.

Prelims focus

  • Akota is near Vadodara and is associated with early medieval Jain bronze images.
  • The Akota bronzes include representations of Adinatha, Parshvanatha and Mahavira.
  • Lost-wax casting was an important method used for producing bronze images.
  • Shatrunjaya is associated with Adinatha; Girnar with Neminatha; Taranga with Ajitanatha.
  • Valabhi is associated with Shvetambara canonical compilation, while Patan is associated with Hemachandra and manuscript learning.
  • Trap: Akota's bronze sculptures are not the same heritage as Valabhi's textual compilation or Palitana's hill temples.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, 'Temple Architecture and Sculpture,' printed pp. 94–95; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 7, 'Indian Bronze Sculpture,' printed p. 105; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 7, 'New Questions and Ideas,' printed pp. 69–70; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 4, 'Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings,' printed pp. 88–89.]
